title: Good Reasons, True Belief, and Still Not Knowing

intro.summary: Gettier asks whether knowing something is the same as having a true belief that you have good reasons for, a definition that goes back to Plato and that philosophers such as Chisholm and Ayer had recently stated. He accepts two plausible points: good reasons can support a false belief, and correct logical steps from a well-supported belief carry the support along. Using them, he builds two short imagined cases in which a person has a true, well-supported belief that is true only by luck, so the person plainly does not know it. He concludes that the three conditions are not enough for knowledge, and that the same cases defeat Chisholm's and Ayer's versions. The main limits are that the argument rests on readers sharing the judgement that Smith does not know (some later philosophers have questioned how universal that judgement is) and that Gettier offers no repaired definition. Note that the source text has a page of a different article, Peter Achinstein's 'Circularity and Induction', printed in the middle of it; this lesson does not cover that article. Good follow-up topics this lesson leaves out include the 'no false lemmas' repair, causal theories of knowledge, reliabilism, defeasibility theories, and the wider debate about whether knowledge can be defined at all.
background: Epistemology is the part of philosophy that asks what knowledge is and how we get it.
A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, such as 'Jones owns a Ford'.
For centuries, many philosophers treated knowledge as a true belief backed by good reasons, a view often traced to Plato.
Gettier's paper is only about three pages long, yet it changed the course of this field.
intro.aha: You can believe something true, for excellent reasons, and still not know it, because your reasons and the truth line up only by luck.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: What does it take to know something, rather than just guess right? A popular answer is a three-part recipe: the statement must be true, you must believe it, and you must have good reasons (be 'justified') for believing it. Gettier asks whether meeting those three conditions is really enough to count as knowing.
primer.quote: (a) S knows that P IFF (i) P is true, (ii) S believes that P, and (iii) S is justified in believing that P.

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: Gettier ran no experiment. He made an argument using imagined stories, called thought experiments. He started from two points most people accept. First, you can have good reasons for a belief that turns out false. Second, if you correctly reason from a well-supported belief to something it guarantees, the new belief is well supported too.
primer.quote: it is possible for a person to be justified in believing a proposition that is in fact false.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: He told two stories about a man named Smith. In each story Smith reasons well from strong evidence, but his evidence points at a false statement. By coincidence, the conclusion he draws is true anyway. Smith's belief is true, believed and justified, yet nobody would say he knows it, because it is right only by luck.
primer.quote: If these two conditions hold then Smith does not know that (h) is true, even though (i) (h) is true, (ii) Smith does believe that (h) is true, and (iii) Smith is justified in believing that (h) is true.

primer.heading: Why it matters and its limits
primer.body: If even one case meets all three conditions without being knowledge, the recipe is not enough. Gettier says the same cases also defeat the versions stated by Chisholm and Ayer. His paper set off decades of attempts to add a fourth condition. The argument depends on readers agreeing that Smith does not know, and Gettier does not say what the missing ingredient is.

concepts.title: Needed versus enough
concepts.idea: A condition is necessary if you can't have the thing without it, and sufficient if having it guarantees the thing; a definition claims its conditions are both.

terms.means: Something you cannot have the thing without; it is needed, though it may not be enough on its own
Something that guarantees the thing whenever it holds; it is enough, though it may not be the only way
A single case that shows a general claim is false

concepts.recap: Needed means no thing without it; enough means it guarantees the thing. One case where all the conditions hold but the thing is missing shows they are not enough.

understand.explanation: A necessary condition is something you cannot have the thing without: you can't get into a concert without a ticket. A sufficient condition is something that guarantees the thing: anything that is a square is certainly a rectangle. Some conditions are needed but not enough, and others are enough but not needed. A definition says 'X if and only if these conditions hold', which claims its conditions are both necessary and, taken together, sufficient. So a single counterexample can sink it: a case that has the thing but lacks a condition shows that condition is not necessary, and a case where every condition holds but the thing is missing shows the conditions are not sufficient. Gettier's 1963 paper looks at definitions of knowing stated in exactly this form and argues that their conditions are not enough.
understand.quote: attempts have been made in recent years to state necessary and sufficient conditions for someone's knowing a given proposition.

activities.prompt: Two everyday cases. For each one, ask two questions: can you have the result without the condition? Does the condition guarantee the result?

cases.label: A concert ticket
cases.text: You can't get into the concert without a ticket, so the ticket is needed (necessary). But a ticket alone doesn't guarantee you get in: you could arrive after the doors close, or the show could be cancelled. So it is not enough (not sufficient).

cases.label: Square and rectangle
cases.text: Every square is a rectangle (four straight sides, four right angles), so being a square is enough (sufficient) for being a rectangle. But a long, thin rectangle is not a square, so being a square is not needed (not necessary).

activities.takeaway: Needed and enough are separate questions. A condition can be one without the other. A good definition must pass both tests at once.

activities.title: Needed, enough or both?
activities.prompt: Each card pairs a condition with a result (condition → result). Put each card in the group where it belongs.

cards.text: A plant gets water → the plant grows
cards.feedback: No plant grows without water, so water is needed. But water alone isn't enough: the plant also needs light, for example.

cards.text: There is fuel in the tank → the car starts
cards.feedback: A petrol car won't start without fuel, so fuel is needed. A flat battery can still stop it, so fuel is not enough.

cards.text: You are 18 or older → you can vote (in a country that also requires citizenship)
cards.feedback: In this made-up country you can't vote under 18, so age is needed. A non-citizen over 18 still can't vote, so age is not enough.

cards.text: The animal is a dog → the animal is a mammal
cards.feedback: Every dog is a mammal, so being a dog is enough. Cats and whales are mammals too, so being a dog is not needed.

cards.text: You live in Paris → you live in France
cards.feedback: Living in Paris guarantees living in France, so it is enough. People in Lyon live in France too, so living in Paris is not needed.

cards.text: You score 100% on a test with a 50% pass mark → you pass
cards.feedback: A perfect score guarantees a pass, so it is enough. A score of 60% also passes, so a perfect score is not needed.

cards.text: A flat shape is closed and made of exactly three straight sides → it is a triangle
cards.feedback: No triangle lacks this, and every such shape is a triangle. It works in both directions, which is what a good definition does.

cards.text: A whole number ends in 0 → it divides exactly by 10
cards.feedback: Every whole number ending in 0 divides by 10, and every whole number that divides by 10 ends in 0. It is both needed and enough.

activities.takeaway: Ask both questions every time. 'Can I have the result without it?' tests needed. 'Does it guarantee the result?' tests enough. Only cards that pass both tests could serve as a definition.

activities.question: Someone proposes a definition: a person is a doctor if and only if they (1) wear a white coat, (2) work in a hospital and (3) carry a stethoscope. Maria is a nurse who does all three, but she is not a doctor. What does Maria's case show?

options.text: The three conditions together are not enough: they are not sufficient for being a doctor.
options.feedback: Right. Every condition holds for Maria, yet she is not a doctor. One case like this shows the conditions do not guarantee the result.

options.text: One of the three conditions is not needed for being a doctor.
options.feedback: Not from this case. Maria meets every condition. To show a condition isn't needed, you would need a doctor who lacks it.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because Maria meets all three conditions.
options.feedback: That is exactly the problem. The definition says anyone who meets all three is a doctor. Maria meets all three but isn't one, so the definition gives the wrong answer for her.

options.text: One nurse isn't enough; we would need many cases like Maria's before the definition fails.
options.feedback: A definition claims to hold in every case, so one clear counterexample is enough to show it is false. More cases like Maria's would not make it any more false.

hints: Check Maria against each condition. Does she meet them?
She meets all three, yet she is not a doctor. Does that test 'needed' or 'enough'?

activities.question: Take the same definition. Dr Lee is a real doctor. On a home visit she wears jeans and no white coat. What does this case show?

options.text: The three conditions together are not enough.
options.feedback: No. To show the conditions aren't enough, you need someone who meets them all but isn't a doctor, like Maria. Dr Lee doesn't meet them all.

options.text: Wearing a white coat is not needed for being a doctor.
options.feedback: Right. Here is a doctor without a white coat, so the coat is not a necessary condition. This is the other way a single counterexample can break a definition.

options.text: Nothing, because Dr Lee is still a doctor.
options.feedback: The fact that she is still a doctor is the key. The definition says no one without a white coat is a doctor. She is one, so the definition is wrong about her.

options.text: Dr Lee isn't really a doctor while she is out of her white coat.
options.feedback: That bends the facts to save the definition. Her job doesn't change with her clothes, so the definition has to give way, not the case.

hints: Is Dr Lee a doctor? Does she meet every condition?
She has the result without one of the conditions. Which test does that fail: 'needed' or 'enough'?

concepts.title: The three-part recipe for knowing
concepts.idea: The traditional definition says you know a statement exactly when it is true, you believe it, and you are justified in believing it.

predict.question: Someone proposes a shorter recipe: 'You know a statement when it is true and you believe it.' The good-reasons part is dropped. Which case would the shorter recipe count as knowing, but the three-part recipe would not?
options: Guessing that a coin will land heads, and it does
Believing, on a reliable weather report, that it will rain, when it then stays dry
A fact about your town that you have never thought about
Checking the timetable, believing the train leaves at 8:15, and it does
why: Correct. The guess is true and believed, so the shorter recipe says 'knows'. It has no good reasons, so the three-part recipe says no. The reasons ingredient is what rules out lucky guesses.
It is tempting because the reasons are good. But the statement is false, and both recipes require truth. Neither recipe counts it.
You might pick this because the fact is true. But you don't believe it, since you have never considered it. Both recipes need belief, so neither counts it.
This one has all three ingredients, so both recipes count it as knowing. Dropping the reasons part only changes cases where the reasons are missing.

terms.means: A belief that is true and held for good reasons: the three ingredients of the traditional recipe for knowing
An attempt to say exactly which conditions are needed for knowing, and which together are enough

model.title: Three switches and one verdict: does this count as knowing?
model.note: Teaching model: each ingredient is a simple yes/no switch. Real truth, belief and reasons can be partial, uncertain or disputed. The 1s and 0s mean yes and no. They are not data from the paper.

controls.label: The person has good reasons for it

steps.say: Take an everyday statement, such as 'the café opens at 9'. This grid checks whether someone knows it. The top three rows are ingredients. The bottom row is the verdict.
This switch says whether the statement is actually true, in the world.
This one says whether the person believes it, meaning they take it to be true.
This one says whether they have good reasons, such as having read the café's sign.
This box counts how many ingredients are present. Watch the verdict row as you flip the switches.

explore.prompt: Flip the switches and watch the verdict row. Look for situations that come close to knowing but miss.

goals.text: Make the statement true and give the person good reasons, but still get a verdict of 'not knowing'.
hints: The recipe needs every ingredient. Which one could still be missing?
Two ingredients are about the world and the evidence. One is about what goes on in the person's head.
Picture someone holding the café's sign in their hand who still thinks it opens at 10.

goals.text: Set up a lucky guess: someone takes a statement to be true, and it is true, but they have no grounds for it.
hints: What makes a guess a guess, and not an informed judgement?
A guess can be right, and the guesser can believe it. One ingredient is still absent.
Leave the reasons switch where a guesser would have it, then check the verdict row.

feedback.correct: Right. A lucky guess is true and believed but has no good reasons. Dropping the reasons ingredient would let it count as knowing. The three-part recipe keeps it out.
feedback.incorrect: Compare each case against both recipes. Only the reasons ingredient differs between them. So look for the case that is true and believed but has no good reasons behind it, which is a lucky guess.

steps.say: Start with nothing in place. No ingredients, so the verdict is 0: this does not count as knowing.
Give the person good reasons: they read the café's sign. That is one ingredient. The verdict is still 0.
Now they also believe it. That makes two ingredients, and the verdict is still 0. The statement isn't true yet, because the sign could be out of date.
Make the statement true. With all three ingredients present, the verdict lights up. This combination has a name: justified true belief.
The recipe is all or nothing. Switch truth off, and the verdict drops to 0 even though belief and reasons stay. So each ingredient is needed.
The recipe also claims the reverse: whenever all three are present, that is enough for knowing.
Needed and enough together: that is a full analysis of knowledge. Keep this lit-up state in mind. The rest of the lesson asks whether it really is enough.

understand.explanation: The traditional recipe says you know a statement exactly when three things hold. The statement is true, you believe it, and you have good reasons for believing it. Each ingredient is meant to be needed. Without truth you have only a mistake. Without belief you have a fact you don't hold. Without reasons you have a lucky guess. Together they are meant to be enough. Gettier writes the recipe out in this form and notes two close versions: Chisholm's uses 'adequate evidence', and Ayer's uses 'the right to be sure'. He sets it out so that he can test whether the three ingredients really are enough. The yes/no switches here simplify things, because real reasons and beliefs come in degrees.
understand.quote: S knows that P IFF (i) P is true, (ii) S believes that P, and (iii) S is justified in believing that P.

equation.text: S is justified in believing that P

connect.caption: This is Gettier's definition (a), word for word. S is the person and P is the statement. IFF means 'if and only if'. The red part is the verdict row. The three coloured conditions are the three switches. In the model, the verdict equals truth × belief × reasons, so it is 1 only when all three are 1.

concepts.recap: On the traditional recipe, knowing means having all three: a true statement, your belief in it, and good reasons for that belief.

concepts.title: Good reasons can point to a false belief
concepts.idea: Being justified means having strong evidence, and strong evidence can still support a belief that turns out false.

terms.means: Able to be mistaken. Fallible evidence is good evidence that can still point the wrong way.

concepts.recap: Justified and true are two separate checks: strong reasons can back a false belief, and a true belief can rest on no good reasons at all.

understand.explanation: To be justified in believing something means to have good reasons or strong evidence for it, the kind a careful, sensible person would rely on. Even strong evidence can mislead: a reliable forecast can be wrong, and a trustworthy friend can be honestly mistaken. So justification is fallible, which means it can be wrong. You can be fully justified and still believe something false. Gettier sets this down as the first of two starting points for his argument, and he means the same sense of 'justified' that the three-part recipe for knowing uses. He states it as an assumption rather than proving it. Most philosophers accept it, though some argue that real knowledge needs reasons that cannot fail.
understand.quote: it is possible for a person to be justified in believing a proposition that is in fact false.
understand.quote_where: Page 121, the first of the two points noted before Case I

activities.prompt: Two everyday beliefs. Check each one twice: does the person have good reasons (justified)? Does the belief match the facts (true)?

cases.label: Strong reasons, false belief
cases.text: Maya sees her flatmate's car in the driveway, his keys on the hook and his coat by the door. She believes: 'Sam is home.' Every clue points that way. In fact a friend picked Sam up twenty minutes ago and he is out. Maya is justified, but her belief is false.

cases.label: No real reasons, true belief
cases.text: Leo's knee itches, and he declares: 'It will rain this afternoon.' An itchy knee is no evidence about the weather. It does rain that afternoon. Leo's belief is true, but he is not justified in it.

activities.takeaway: The two checks come apart in both directions. Good reasons do not guarantee truth, and truth does not show there were good reasons. That is why the recipe for knowing lists them as separate conditions.

activities.title: Justified? True? Sort the beliefs
activities.prompt: For each belief, ask two questions: did the person have good reasons for it, and did it turn out to match the facts? Drop each card in the group that fits.

cards.text: A trusted weather service gives a 90% chance of rain. Priya believes it will rain today. The day stays dry.
cards.feedback: A 90% forecast from a reliable service is strong evidence, so Priya is justified. The forecast still missed, so her belief is false. Good evidence is fallible.

cards.text: The kitchen clock has always kept good time, and Ben has no reason to doubt it. It reads 3:00, so he believes it is 3:00. The clock stopped yesterday, and it is really 5:40.
cards.feedback: A clock that has always worked gives Ben a good reason, so he is justified. The clock has stopped, so his belief is false. His reasons were fine. The world simply let them down.

cards.text: Ben knows the kitchen clock stopped a week ago, but he trusts it anyway. It reads 3:00, and by chance it really is 3:00.
cards.feedback: The belief is true, but Ben knows the clock is broken, so reading it gives him no good reason. Compare the previous clock card: the same clock reading, but the reasons are very different.

cards.text: Ana dreamed about the number 17, so she believes 17 will win tonight's raffle. It wins.
cards.feedback: A dream is not evidence about a raffle draw, so Ana is not justified. The belief happened to be true, but truth alone does not make a belief justified.

cards.text: Omar checks a working station clock that reads 5:40 and believes it is 5:40. It is 5:40.
cards.feedback: A working clock is a good reason, and the belief matches the facts, so both checks pass. This is the ordinary case where justification and truth line up.

cards.text: The trusted weather service gives a 90% chance of rain. Priya believes it will rain, and it does.
cards.feedback: The same strong evidence as the dry-day card, and this time the world cooperates. Notice that Priya's reasons were identical in both cards. Only the outcome changed.

cards.text: On a hunch, with no tracking update, Kim believes her parcel arrived today. It hasn't.
cards.feedback: A hunch is not a good reason, so Kim is not justified, and the parcel has not come, so her belief is false. It fails both checks.

cards.text: Tom believes the café is open because 'it just feels like an open day'. It is closed for a holiday.
cards.feedback: A feeling about the day gives no real evidence, so Tom is not justified, and the café is shut, so his belief is false. It fails both checks.

hints: Ask the two questions separately: first 'were the reasons good?', then 'did it turn out true?'
Whether a belief is justified depends only on what the person had to go on, not on how things turned out.
Two cards share the same clock, and two share the same forecast. Same reasons can sit in different groups when the outcome differs.
activities.takeaway: Whether you are justified depends on your reasons. Whether your belief is true depends on the world. Because strong reasons can still point to a falsehood, being justified never guarantees being right.

concepts.title: Reasons flow through correct logic
concepts.idea: If you are justified in believing a statement and you correctly deduce something it guarantees, you are justified in the new statement too, even when the starting statement is false.

terms.means: One statement entails another when, whenever the first is true, the second must be true too
An either-or statement, 'A or B', which is true when at least one of its two parts is true

concepts.recap: Good reasons pass along correct logic: if you're justified in believing P and you correctly deduce Q from it, you're justified in believing Q, even if P later turns out to be false.

understand.explanation: Gettier's second starting point is about how good reasons get passed along. One statement entails another when, whenever the first is true, the second must be true too. For example, 'Jones owns a Ford' entails a disjunction, an either-or statement such as 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston', because that kind of statement needs only one true part. If you are justified in believing the first statement, correctly work out that it guarantees the second, and believe the second for that reason, then you are justified in believing the second too. This holds even if the first statement is false, because strong evidence can back a false belief, so justification can travel down a chain of correct reasoning from a false starting point. Gettier states this as an assumption rather than proving it, and it is widely accepted, but philosophers still debate exactly how such principles should be stated.
understand.quote: Secondly, for any proposition P, if S is justified in believing P, and P entails Q, and S deduces Q from P and accepts Q as a result of this deduction, then S is justified in believing Q.
understand.quote_where: Opening section, the second of two points noted just before Case I

activities.title: From a Ford to Boston: following Smith's reasoning

steps.text: Start with Smith's evidence. As far back as he remembers, Jones has always owned a car, and always a Ford. Jones has also just offered Smith a ride while driving a Ford.
Based on that evidence, Smith believes statement (f): 'Jones owns a Ford.' His reasons are good, so he is justified in believing it.

Smith picks a place-name at random and builds a disjunction, an either-or statement: (g) 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston.' A disjunction is true when at least one of its two parts is true.
So if (f) is true, (g) must be true, wherever Brown actually is. This guarantee is what it means for (f) to entail (g).
Smith sees this link and accepts (g) because of (f). By Gettier's second point, his justification for (f) passes on to (g).
Smith has no idea where Brown is. That does not matter here. His reason for believing (g) comes entirely from (f), not from any clue about Boston.
Now suppose, without Smith knowing it, that Jones does not own a Ford after all. Smith's evidence was still strong, so he was still justified in (f), and therefore still justified in (g).
steps.result: Justification survives a false starting point

activities.takeaway: Justification follows the line of correct reasoning, not the facts. A well-supported belief passes its support to anything you correctly deduce from it, even if the belief itself is false.

activities.title: What does 'Jones owns a Ford' guarantee?
activities.prompt: Suppose (f) 'Jones owns a Ford' is true. Sort each statement: must it then be true, or could it still be false?

groups.label: Not guaranteed: could still be false

cards.text: Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston.
cards.feedback: Guaranteed. A disjunction needs only one true part, and (f) supplies it. This is Gettier's statement (g).

cards.text: Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona.
cards.feedback: Guaranteed, for the same reason. Swapping the place-name changes nothing, because the first part already makes the whole statement true. This is Gettier's (h).

cards.text: Jones owns a car.
cards.feedback: Guaranteed. Every Ford is a car, so if Jones owns a Ford, he owns a car.

cards.text: Brown is in Boston.
cards.feedback: Not guaranteed. (f) is about Jones, not Brown. Brown could be anywhere.

cards.text: Jones owns a Ford, and Brown is in Boston.
cards.feedback: Not guaranteed. An 'and' statement needs both parts true, and (f) says nothing about Brown. Compare this with the 'or' version, which only needs one part.

cards.text: Jones owns a blue Ford.
cards.feedback: Not guaranteed. This adds a detail that (f) doesn't contain. The Ford could be any colour.

activities.takeaway: A statement follows from (f) only if (f) being true leaves no way for it to be false. Disjunctions built on (f) always pass this test. 'And' statements, and statements that add new details, do not.
hints: For each card, ask whether it could be false even if Jones really does own a Ford.
'Or' needs one true part, while 'and' needs both. Which part does (f) give you for free?

activities.prompt: Trace the route along which Smith's justification travels, from his evidence to his belief in (g): 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston.'

nodes.label: Evidence: Jones always drove a Ford
Belief (g): Ford, or Brown in Boston

activities.explanation: Smith's justification starts with his evidence about Jones and supports belief (f). It then passes through his correct deduction to belief (g). 'Clues about where Brown is' cannot be on the route, because the paper says Smith has no idea where Brown is: that box is empty. The randomly picked place-name only fills in the second half of (g). It adds no support, because a random guess is not a reason. All of the support for (g) flows through (f).
hints: Start from what gives Smith good reasons in the first place.
Smith knows nothing about Brown's whereabouts, and a random pick is not evidence. Which boxes does that rule out?
The route goes through both of Smith's beliefs, with his deduction in between.

concepts.title: Case I: the job and the ten coins
concepts.idea: Smith's belief that 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket' is true and justified, but what makes it true (his own coins) is not what his reasons were about (Jones's coins).

terms.means: A statement that joins two claims with 'and'. It is true only if both halves are true.
A case that meets all of a definition's conditions but is not an example of the thing being defined.

concepts.recap: In Case I, Smith's true, justified belief is made true by his own pocket while his reasons are about Jones's pocket, so the three-part recipe is met without knowledge.

understand.explanation: Gettier tells a short story. Smith has strong reasons to believe 'Jones will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket'. This is one statement built from two claims joined by 'and', and it is true only if both halves are true; such a statement is called a conjunction. From it Smith correctly deduces (e), 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket', so he believes (e) and is justified in it. In fact Smith himself gets the job and, without knowing it, also has ten coins, so (e) is true and all three parts of the recipe are met. Yet Smith seems not to know (e), because his reasons are about Jones's pocket while what makes (e) true is Smith's own pocket. A case like this meets a definition's conditions but lacks the thing being defined, and is called a counterexample; note that it works only if the reader shares Gettier's judgment that Smith does not know, which the paper states as clear rather than proving.
understand.quote: But it is equally clear that Smith does not know that (e) is true; for (e) is true in virtue of the number of coins in Smith's pocket, while Smith does not know how many coins are in Smith's pocket, and bases his belief in (e) on a count of the coins in Jones's pocket, whom he falsely believes to be the man who will get the job.

activities.prompt: Follow Gettier's Case I one step at a time. After each step, ask: what does Smith believe, and why?

stages.label: The setup
stages.text: Smith and Jones have both applied for the same job. Only one of them will get it.

stages.label: Smith's evidence
stages.text: The company president has assured Smith that Jones will be selected. Ten minutes ago Smith counted the coins in Jones's pocket and found ten. So Smith has strong evidence for (d): 'Jones is the man who will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket.' Statement (d) is a conjunction: two claims joined by 'and'.

stages.label: Smith reasons onward
stages.text: (d) guarantees (e): 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.' Smith sees this and accepts (e) because of (d). By the earlier point that correct deduction carries justification along, Smith is justified in believing (e).

stages.label: First twist
stages.text: Unknown to Smith, he himself, not Jones, will get the job. So the first half of (d) is false, and that makes the whole of (d) false.

stages.label: Second twist
stages.text: Also unknown to Smith, he himself happens to have ten coins in his pocket. So the man who will get the job (Smith) does have ten coins. Statement (e) is true.

stages.label: The tally
stages.text: (e) is true. Smith believes (e). Smith is justified in believing (e). Every part of the three-part recipe is met. Yet Smith's reasons were all about Jones, and the fact that makes (e) true is in Smith's own pocket, which he never checked.

activities.takeaway: Smith's belief is true, believed and justified, but the facts it rests on and the facts that make it true are different facts.

activities.prompt: The diagram shows everything connected to statement (e). Select every node that Smith's belief in (e) actually rests on: the reasons he used to reach it.

nodes.label: Smith has 10 coins in his pocket

activities.explanation: Smith's belief in (e) rests on (d), and (d) rests on two pieces of evidence: the president's assurance and his own count of Jones's coins. Every one of these is about Jones. The two bottom nodes, 'Smith will get the job' and 'Smith has 10 coins', are facts Smith knows nothing about, so they play no part in his reasoning.
hints: Think only about what Smith himself had in mind when he accepted (e).
Smith did not know he would get the job, or how many coins were in his own pocket.
His reasoning ran from two pieces of evidence, through one statement, to (e).

activities.prompt: Same diagram, new question. Select the facts that actually make (e) true in the story.

nodes.label: Smith has 10 coins in his pocket

activities.explanation: (e) says the job-winner has ten coins. The job-winner is Smith, and Smith has ten coins, so those two facts make (e) true. Statement (d) cannot be what makes (e) true, because (d) is false: Jones does not get the job. Compare this answer with the last one: the two sets share no node at all. That gap is the whole point of the case.
hints: Ask who really gets the job, and whose pocket then matters.
Statement (d) turned out to be false, so it cannot be what makes (e) true.

activities.question: According to Gettier, does Smith know (e), 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'? Pick the answer and the reason that the paper gives.

options.text: Yes: (e) is true, Smith believes it, and he is justified, so he knows it.
options.feedback: That is what the three-part recipe would say, and it is exactly the verdict Gettier rejects. All three conditions hold here, yet he says it is 'equally clear that Smith does not know'. If you agree with him, the recipe gives the wrong answer in this case.
Look again at the second twist: Smith gets the job and has ten coins, so (e) is true. What is false is (d), the statement about Jones that Smith started from.

options.text: No, because Smith is not justified in believing (e).
options.feedback: Smith has strong evidence for (d) and correctly deduces (e) from it, so he is justified. Gettier stresses this: 'Smith is clearly justified in believing that (e) is true.' The problem lies elsewhere.

options.text: No, because (e) is made true by Smith's own coins, while his reasons were about Jones's coins.
options.feedback: Right. All three conditions are met, but the facts that make (e) true and the facts his reasons rest on do not overlap. That is the gap Gettier points to, and it makes Case I a counterexample to the claim that the three conditions are enough for knowledge.

concepts.title: Case II: true by sheer coincidence
concepts.idea: When Smith's starting belief is false, whether his well-reasoned 'either Jones owns a Ford or Brown is in X' is true depends only on where Brown happens to be, so meeting all three conditions can be pure luck and the recipe is not enough.

predict.question: Imagine Mia glances at the hall clock, which has kept perfect time for years, and reads 3:00. Unknown to her, it stopped yesterday at exactly 3:00, and it happens to be 3:00 right now. Which part of the three-part recipe fails for her belief 'it is 3:00'?
options: None of them: it is true, she believes it, she is justified, yet she got it right by luck
Truth: her belief isn't really true
Belief: she doesn't really believe it
Justification: a stopped clock gives her no reason at all
why: Right. Like Smith in Case II, Mia meets all three conditions. What makes her belief true (the actual time) has nothing to do with what her reason was about (a clock she thinks is working), so it lines up only by chance.
It might feel wrong to call it true, but it really is 3:00. Truth is about the world, not about how she found out. That is why the case is a problem: the truth condition is met.
She does believe it. She reads the clock and forms the belief, just as Smith accepts (h). The belief condition is met.

Tempting, but justification is about her evidence, not about hidden facts. She has years of good experience with the clock and no hint it stopped. Good reasons can rest on something false, as with Smith's belief about the Ford.

terms.means: An either-or statement. It is true when at least one of its two halves is true.
When a belief comes out true by chance, not because of the reasons the person had for it.
A case where someone has a true, justified belief that still does not seem to be knowledge.

model.title: Smith's statements: which are true, believed and justified?
model.note: Teaching model: it shows only the facts from Gettier's Case II. 1 means yes and 0 means no. Belief and justification are fixed at yes, because the paper stipulates them. 'Somewhere else' is an added option standing for any place Smith didn't name. These are the story's own yes/no facts, not measurements or data.

controls.label: Where Brown really is (0 Boston, 1 Barcelona, 2 Brest-Litovsk, 3 somewhere else)

outputs.label: Either-or lines meeting all three conditions
Lines true only because of where Brown is

rows.label: (g) Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston
(h) Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona
(i) Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Brest-Litovsk

steps.say: Each row is one statement Smith believes. The columns ask three things about it: is it true, does Smith believe it, is he justified? 1 means yes, 0 means no.
This switch says whether Jones really owns a Ford. That is Smith's one reason for every row.
This slider says where Brown really is. Smith has no idea. He picked three city names at random.
Watch it move from Boston to Barcelona to Brest-Litovsk, and then to a place Smith never named.
These two counts show how many either-or lines meet all three conditions, and how many are true only because of where Brown is.

explore.prompt: Now you run the story. Decide what the world is like and see which of Smith's lines come out true, and why.

goals.text: Make Smith's Boston statement true in a way his reason plays no part in.
hints: What was Smith's reason for believing all three lines?
Take his reason away first. Then ask what else could make the Boston line true.
With the Ford gone, only Brown's real location can make that line true.

goals.text: Make every one of Smith's three either-or lines false, while he still believes each one and is justified in it.
hints: When is an either-or statement false?
Both halves must be false: the Ford half and the Brown half.
Brown has to be somewhere none of Smith's lines mentions.

feedback.correct: Yes. Mia's belief is true, believed and justified, just like Smith's (h). But her reason (a clock she trusts) and the truth (the actual time) meet only by coincidence. That is the pattern Gettier found: all three conditions can hold by luck.
feedback.incorrect: You probably expected one of the three conditions to break, since something has clearly gone wrong. But each one holds: it is 3:00, she believes it, and her trust in the clock is well founded. What has gone wrong is the link between her reasons and the truth, and the recipe doesn't check that link.

steps.say: Start where Smith thinks the world is: Jones owns a Ford, and Brown is somewhere unnamed. Each line is an either-or statement, called a disjunction. It is true if at least one half is true, so the Ford half makes all three true.
Move Brown to Boston. Nothing changes. While the Ford is real, the Ford half carries every line, and Smith's reason is what makes them true.

Look at the belief and justification columns. They never move. Smith inferred each line correctly from a belief he had strong evidence for, so his reasons stay just as good whatever the world is really like.

Now Gettier's twist: Jones is driving a rented car and owns no Ford. Switch it off. With Brown somewhere unnamed, all three lines are false, though Smith still believes them for the same good reasons.
Move Brown to Boston. Now (g) is true. Nothing about Smith changed. Only Brown's location, which Smith knows nothing about, decided it.
This is Gettier's actual story: Brown is in Barcelona, so (h) is true. True, believed, justified, but true for a reason that has nothing to do with Smith's evidence. That is epistemic luck.

A case where all three conditions hold and knowledge still seems missing is called a Gettier case. You can believe something true, for excellent reasons, and still not know it, because your reasons and the truth line up only by luck.

understand.explanation: In Case II, Smith has strong evidence that Jones owns a Ford, and he correctly infers three either-or statements from it, so he is justified in all three. Once the Ford turns out to be rented, the only thing that can make any of them true is where Brown is, and Smith picked those cities at random. Brown happens to be in Barcelona, so (h) is true, believed and justified, yet Gettier judges that Smith plainly does not know it. Since all three conditions hold without knowledge, they are not sufficient for knowing. Note how the argument works: it relies on the reader agreeing that Smith doesn't know. It also only shows the conditions aren't enough together. It does not claim any of them is unnecessary.
understand.quote: If these two conditions hold then Smith does not know that (h) is true, even though (i) (h) is true, (ii) Smith does believe that (h) is true, and (iii) Smith is justified in believing that (h) is true.

check.task: Put the model in a state where Smith's Brest-Litovsk statement meets all three conditions, yet, like (h) in Gettier's story, he does not know it.
check.hint: If the Ford is real, Smith's reason makes the line true, and nothing is lucky. What has to go, and what then has to make the line true?
check.misconception: That any true, justified belief is knowledge, or that the luck lies in Smith's reasoning. His reasoning is the same in every state. Luck enters only when his reason is false and Brown's location alone decides the truth.

connect.caption: Gettier's paper has no formula here. This is the model's rule: the ordinary truth rule for an either-or statement, applied to his proposition (h). The blue part is Smith's reason (the Ford switch). The orange part is Brown's real location (the city slider). With the Ford off, only the orange part can make (h) true, and Smith knows nothing about it.

concepts.recap: Smith's either-or belief was true, believed and justified, yet true only because of where Brown happened to be, so the three conditions are not enough for knowing.

activities.prompt: Gettier says his cases also defeat two other famous definitions. Match each wording to the definition it comes from.

pairs.text: S is justified in believing that P
pairs.target: The standard recipe (a): the reasons condition
pairs.feedback: This is the condition Smith meets for (h) by correctly inferring it from his well-supported belief about the Ford.

pairs.text: S has adequate evidence for P
pairs.feedback: Smith has adequate evidence for (h): strong evidence for (f), passed on by a correct inference. Chisholm's conditions are met, and still Smith doesn't know.

pairs.text: S has the right to be sure that P is true
pairs.feedback: Given his evidence, Smith has every right to be sure of (h). Ayer's condition holds too, and the luck remains.
Chisholm's word for believing. Smith accepts (h) on the basis of (f), as the story says.

pairs.text: S is sure that P is true
pairs.feedback: Ayer asks for more than belief: being sure. Smith, trusting his evidence, can be sure, and the case still works.

activities.takeaway: The three definitions use different words for belief and for good reasons, but Smith meets every version in Case II. That is why Gettier says the same cases, 'with appropriate changes', defeat (b) and (c) too. He asserts this rather than spelling out each change, and he aims only at sufficiency: none of these definitions is shown to have an unnecessary condition.
